How do you keep your knives sharp?
i've tried a metal honing rod (don't know what they're called) but it didn't really make a difference

Honing rods are for straightening your blade, not for sharpening it.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honing_steel
Everything (mostly) that you never wanted to know about knives, courtesy of Good Eats. (Start at 5:20)
thank you for the link, The Show is quite funny

I second that. I cooked professionally and to this day I have never taken my knives to a professional sharpener. I use three stones, the first two are water and the last is oil. There are a lot of videos out there showing how to sharpen knives using stones. But once you have sharpened your knives, lock them away so that only you use them. Serious cooks never share their knives.

If using a dry stone, one may then choose to proceed to utilize oil. Or remain with a dry stone.

Once one has sharpened a knife with a wet whetstone, it must always be sharpened with a wet whetstone.

Knife storage, cutting surface, and honing technique are key.

Don't store your knives vertically in a knife block, but rather in a horizontal knife block or a magnetic strip (this is a point of some contention, some argue that the metal strips can dull a knife, but it would be minimal. If you're concerned get a wooden one like the photo).

Never cut on glass or stone, plastic is better if it's all you have, but wood is best. For the best cutting surface get an end-grain cutting board.

Every time you go to use your knife run it at a 20 degree angle to a honing steel 3-4 times a side, just to maintain the edge.

Get the knife professionally sharpened once or twice a year, any good kitchen store should be able to do it for pretty cheap.

Oh, and always wash it by hand and dry it immediately. Never put it in the dishwasher.
If you need to store your knives temporarily in a vertical block, do so with the sharp edge of the blade up.

My prefered blade for almost everything is a cheap asian cleaver. $8-$15. Hone them as per good eats before and after each use and store them correctly and the should stay tomato sharp for 2-3 years. Use the older ones for less delicate work like meat, bones, and then sharpen them with a stone, or even the sharpener on the back of a can opener. That sounds blasphemous to many, but these are cheap and old knives I am suggesting doing this with.

Good knives are expensive and require a lot of care. Unless you want to become proficient in sharpening you will need to send the knives out. I have a friend who actually has sharpening parties. Bring some weed and beer and he'll sharpen all your shit. Friends like these are accidentally acquired as part of life tho.

Cheap knives, over time, will cost about the same, but will allow you to replace knives you may have grown tired of, accumulate more knives that you will task for different things, and so on.

Cutting boards... These days I use only plastic cutting boards. I have some larger ones and a bunch of folding ones. These are awesome because you can change surfaces quickly or stage your ingredients on them, use them as funnels, etc. and then toss them into the dishwasher. Cheap enough when they are tired you can toss them or put them in with your camping gear. Glass is stupid for obvious reasons.

Even when chopping slide the blade when possible.

I love the asian cleaver because it slides up and down your hand/finger offering mad control. With practice you can peel potatoes or debone a chicken, but I generally use the appropriate tool for that now. Enough heft to cut through the bones of a whole duck or chicken.
